claim: localhost's release pipeline: push a vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH tag → release.yml validates the tag regex, builds macOS DMG + Linux deb/rpm/AppImage + Windows NSIS installer in parallel jobs, and creates a DRAFT GitHub Release with .sha256 per artifact and notes generated from merged PRs; nothing is public until a maintainer publishes. Publishing re-runs the workflow to update the Homebrew tap.
quote: Pushing a `v*` tag runs the Release workflow... Then it drafts one GitHub Release with all of them, a SHA-256 for each, and notes generated from the merged PRs. Nothing is public until a maintainer publishes the draft.
title: Releasing localhost

claim: Version handling norm demonstrated: the git tag is the single source of version ('The tag is the only place the version lives: v0.3.1 builds version 0.3.1'), SemVer 0.x, tag format enforced in CI ('Tags are vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, nothing else; the workflow rejects any other v* tag'), workflow run number used as build number.
quote: The tag is the only place the version lives: `v0.3.1` builds version `0.3.1` (`CFBundleShortVersionString`), with the workflow's run number as the build number (`CFBundleVersion`)... Tags are `vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`, nothing else; the workflow rejects any other `v*` tag.
title: Releasing localhost

claim: localhost's CI gates PRs with path-filtered jobs so a skipped job reports as passing: 'The gating is a job-level if: on the changes job's outputs, never workflow-level paths:'; jobs run only when their files changed, all must pass to merge, macOS job skips draft PRs to save macOS minutes, every push to main runs everything.
quote: Each job runs on a pull request only when files it depends on changed, and on every push to main. The gating is a job-level `if:` on the `changes` job's outputs, never workflow-level `paths:`: a skipped job reports as passing, so a required check never waits for a run that didn't start.
title: localhost ci.yml

claim: localhost's signing strategy is explicitly tiered and documented: macOS Developer ID+notarization when its 5 secrets exist, else a long-lived self-signed cert (today, needs Open Anyway once), else ad hoc; Windows Authenticode via signtool only when WINDOWS_CERTIFICATE_PFX secrets exist — 'SmartScreen gives a self-signed one no trust, so it does nothing for users. An OV certificate still builds reputation with each download; EV certificates usually live on hardware tokens, which this workflow can't use.'
quote: Use a code signing certificate from a certificate authority: SmartScreen gives a self-signed one no trust, so it does nothing for users. An OV certificate still builds reputation with each download; EV certificates usually live on hardware tokens, which this workflow can't use.
title: Releasing localhost

claim: localhost's release workflow deliberately fails early if updater signing keys are missing ('a release built without them would install fine but could never update itself'), and verifies each private key matches the baked-in public key before publishing — a pattern of making the release pipeline fail loudly rather than shipping a broken updater.
quote: A release without signed updates would leave every user of it on that version for good, so none is built without the keys... The workflow also checks that each private key is the pair of its public key before anything is published.
title: localhost release.yml

claim: dekit (pvolok/dekit, formerly mprocs, MIT, ~2.8k stars, Rust process manager for dev and prod) releases on v* tags with CI that fails if the tag doesn't match the crate version ('tag version $version does not match dekit Cargo version'), treats *-* tags as prereleases (npm_tag=next), and ships install.sh + install.ps1 as release assets alongside per-target tarballs + SHA256SUMS.
quote: if [ "$version" != "$cargo_version" ]; then echo "tag version $version does not match dekit Cargo version $cargo_version" >&2; exit 1; fi ... case "$version" in *-*) prerelease=true; npm_tag=next;; esac

claim: Velopack's official docs codify the SmartScreen reputation model: unsigned builds trigger per-file warnings until that file gains reputation (repeats each release); OV certificates accumulate reputation on the cert so later releases are clean (resets on renewal); EV certificates get instant reputation. Recommended: 'code-sign, prefer an EV (or Azure Artifact Signing) certificate for instant reputation, and expect a short reputation-building period for OV certificates.'
quote: In short: code-sign, prefer an EV (or Azure Artifact Signing) certificate for instant reputation, and expect a short reputation-building period for OV certificates. ... You sign your code with an EV (Extended Validation) certificate. People never get warnings, because EV certificates are granted instant SmartScreen reputation.
location: Velopack docs > Packaging > Code Signing > SmartScreen & Antivirus
title: Code Signing | Velopack

claim: Azure Artifact Signing (formerly Trusted Signing) is the CI-friendly signing path cited for OSS/indie Windows distribution: USD$10/mo, fully cloud-based (no HSM token shipped), automatable in CI pipelines, and its certs get 'built-in instant reputation for smart-screen and defender'. Since June 2023 new code-signing certs can't be downloaded — they must live on a cloud or USB HSM, which breaks classic .pfx-in-GitHub-secrets flows.
quote: Costs USD$10/mo (or USD$120/yr) which is on-par or cheaper than code signing certificates from other issuers. Full cloud solution / Does not require any physical hardware (HSM) shipped to you. Signing can be automated (eg. in your CI pipeline). Artifact Signing certificates get built-in instant reputation for smart-screen and defender. ... since June 1, 2023 ... it is no longer possible to download your code signing certificate. It must be either stored in an authorised cloud HSM or a USB HSM will be shipped to you.
location: Velopack docs > Code Signing > Acquiring a code signing certificate
title: Code Signing | Velopack

claim: PyInstaller's official position is that AV false positives on frozen executables are endemic and unfixable upstream ('this is an indefinite cycle and is why nothing can be done to change PyInstaller'); maintainers close AV reports and redirect to vendor false-positive portals (e.g. Microsoft Defender submission), with only partial mitigations offered: report to vendors, rebuild bootloaders yourself (gcc over MSVC), or buy a code-signing cert which 'is not guaranteed to fix AV false positives but should make them less common.'
quote: Distribution tools like PyInstaller will have malware authors amongst its user base and as a result, machine learning ... based antiviral software respond by blocking anything PyInstaller. ... This is an indefinite cycle and is why nothing can be done to change PyInstaller. ... Purchase codesign certificate for few hundred dollars a year. Note that this is not guaranteed to fix AV false positives but it should make them less common.
title: Antiviral false positive or Trojan detection

claim: PyInstaller's --windowed GUI mode faces *higher* AV detection rates than console mode, not lower — 'it's just a reflection of the fact that most people distributing malware using PyInstaller will be using windowed mode' — so a pywebview GUI exe should expect SmartScreen/AV hits and document them rather than assume a build tweak will fix it.
quote:
# Using `-w/--windowed` mode cause a higher detection rate. Is that a bug?

No, it's just a reflection of the fact that most people distributing malware using PyInstaller will be using windowed mode.
title: Antiviral false positive or Trojan detection

claim: The community-standard PyInstaller release workflow on GitHub Actions is: trigger on push of v* tags, build on a matrix of OS runners (ubuntu/macos/windows-latest), setup-python + pip install pyinstaller, run --onefile (drop --windowed on Windows runners per the canonical example), zip dist/, and attach to the release via softprops/action-gh-release.
quote: I want to setup an action that will build my executable on a new git tag, zip up all the bits from the build and deposit that in a GitHub release for the associated tag. ... on: push: tags: - "v*" ... matrix: os: [ubuntu-latest, macos-latest, windows-latest] ... pyinstaller -n redwrench --onefile --windowed app.py ... - uses: softprops/action-gh-release@v1 with: files: ${{ matrix.os }}-${{github.ref_name}}.zip
title: Building your PyInstaller App for multiple OSs with GitHub Actions

claim: A real-world PyInstaller OSS repo (sukritphiboon/fc-inventory) corroborates the pipeline pattern: its build-release.yml triggers on v*.*.* tags, runs pytest, builds a onedir exe on windows-latest with PyInstaller, computes SHA-256 checksums, publishes via softprops/action-gh-release, and includes an optional Authenticode signing step via azure/trusted-signing-action gated behind the AZURE_SIGNING_ENABLED repo variable — 'signing here (before zipping/hashing) ensures the published checksums cover the signed binary, and removes the Windows SmartScreen warning on first run.'
quote: # Build the standalone .exe automatically when a version tag is pushed, attach it to the GitHub Release, and publish SHA-256 checksums. ... # Optional Authenticode signing via Azure Trusted Signing. No-ops until the repo variable AZURE_SIGNING_ENABLED is set to "true" ... ensures the published checksums cover the signed binary, and removes the Windows SmartScreen warning on first run. ... pyinstaller --noconfirm --onedir --name FCInventoryTool ... uses: softprops/action-gh-release@v2
title: build-release.yml

claim: Interpretation — the release standard for local-dev desktop tools in 2025-26: (1) all community-health files (LICENSE, README, CONTRIBUTING, CODE_OF_CONDUCT, SECURITY, issue+PR templates); (2) v* tag → CI builds all platforms → draft GitHub Release with per-OS artifacts + checksum sidecars + generated notes → maintainer publishes; (3) installers for desktop apps (NSIS/DMG/deb/rpm/AppImage), raw archives+checksums for CLI/TUI tools; (4) tag = version source of truth, enforced in CI; (5) signing optional but documented — unsigned Windows ships with README SmartScreen instructions; (6) a RELEASING.md runbook is the emerging best practice for maintainer-driven releases.
quote: Synthesis of W1-001..W1-026: consistent shape across marcellosso/localhost, F1bonacc1/process-compose, pvolok/dekit, jesseduffield/lazygit, arsenetar/dupeguru.

claim: localhost demonstrates the update-feed pattern: installed apps poll releases/latest/download/latest.json (Tauri) and appcast.xml (Sparkle) — 'Apps read them from releases/latest/download/, so an update reaches users only once its release is published, and a draft or pre-release never' — meaning GitHub Releases doubles as the update server, which is the niche norm for self-updating desktop OSS without a backend.
quote: The release also carries the update feeds that installed apps check: `latest.json` for the Linux and Windows app and `appcast.xml` for the macOS app, both naming this release's packages, each signed with the updater keys... Apps read them from `releases/latest/download/`, so an update reaches users only once its release is published, and a draft or pre-release never.
title: Releasing localhost
